cim: AI isn’t going away. Parents need to teach children how to use it | Opinion
cim_eredeti: AI isn’t going away. Parents need to teach children how to use it | Opinion
szoveg_eredeti:
Most students likely already have access to AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. While some schools embrace them and others restrict them, trying to keep children away from AI is a losing battle. Like it or not, AI will be an important part of their future. The more pressing question is whether we teach children to use it responsibly.

In June 2026, Broward County Public Schools held its first Parent AI Symposium, drawing more than 500 registrants interested in learning how artificial intelligence is changing education. Since then, BCPS has continued the conversation through Family Forums, including a September 2026 session focused on AI in education. The district has also launched its “Broward Powered by AI” initiative, emphasizing responsible AI use, data protection, professional learning for educators and safeguards surrounding the technology.

As an educator, I empathize with parents’ concerns about AI in the classroom. AI can make it remarkably easy for a student to submit work that is not indicative of what the student actually knows. However, banning AI does not teach children how to navigate a world in which the technology will be readily available to them.

BCPS has emphasized that artificial intelligence should enhance learning while keeping people at the center of the educational experience.

There is a crucial distinction between using AI as a tutor and using it as a substitute for learning. A student struggling with a math concept might ask AI to explain it in simpler terms or demonstrate step-by-step strategies. A student studying for a science test might ask AI for a study guide with practice questions based on material covered in class. A developing writer might seek feedback on how to improve an independently written draft. These collaborative efforts keep the student actively engaged in the learning process.

The problem arises when AI produces work for a student rather than helping them create higher-quality work. When a student asks AI to write an essay, answer reading comprehension questions about a story they have never read, or solve an entire math assignment, AI ceases to be a learning tool and becomes a vehicle for cheating.

Parents do not have to become experts in AI to recognize the difference. A simple first step is to ask their children a single question: “Can you show me how you used AI to help you with your homework?”

A practical three-step strategy is to first have students do their homework independently; second, allow them to use AI while being transparent about its use; and third, show them how to verify any AI-generated information. Lori Bruno, a 29-year BCPS middle school teacher, echoes this approach: “I would like parents to encourage their children to do the reading, thinking and learning themselves before turning to AI for help … AI can be useful for checking understanding, asking questions or receiving an additional explanation, but it should not replace the student’s own effort and thinking.”

Responsible AI use also requires students to understand that a confident answer is not necessarily a correct answer. AI tools can produce inaccurate information, misunderstand context and even fabricate information or sources. Children must develop the habit of verifying information generated by AI against reliable sources rather than assuming an answer is correct simply because it sounds authoritative.

Students must also understand that information entered into an AI platform may not necessarily remain private. They should never enter sensitive personal information or identifying information about classmates into an AI prompt. A helpful rule for parents to teach is simple: If you wouldn’t post it on a school bulletin board, don’t type it into an AI prompt.”

Artificial intelligence will continue to become more capable and accessible as today’s students enter college and the workforce. Our responsibility is not to keep children away from AI. It is to ensure that they know how to use it without surrendering the skills that make the technology useful in the first place: curiosity, judgment and independent thinking. AI should be a tool our children know how to use, not a tool they cannot think without.

Christian M. Jacobs is an Ed.D. candidate in educational leadership and Broward County Public Schools teacher with more than 15 years of experience in education in the United States, South Korea, Singapore and Vietnam. He resides in Fort Lauderdale.
